infra.rationale: request/response Next.js app with low ops capacity — lowest-ops target; app on Vercel with managed Postgres is the sanctioned split.
unanswered: existing_cloud (rule 1: a client cloud with procurement and IAM in place)

options.what: Serverless Next.js hosting (functions + edge proxy) with a managed Postgres that branches per preview.
options.why: Request/response Next.js app with low ops capacity and no long-lived process recorded — the lowest-ops target (rule 4).
options.tradeoffs: No long-lived process: websockets, background workers and in-process cron need another service. Two vendors for one app (host + database). Pricing has cliffs at roughly 10x scale.
options.cost_shape: Near-zero at small scale; usage-based with cliffs as traffic and function time grow.

options.what: One long-lived container per service built from the repo, with a platform Postgres on a persistent volume; config as code; migrations run atomically before each release.
options.why: Same low ops as the recommendation, with a long-lived process and flat pricing; costs a little more at zero traffic and gives up native per-PR previews.
options.tradeoffs: Single region; fewer compliance controls than a hyperscaler; per-PR previews are opt-in rather than native; the ecosystem is smaller when you need an unusual add-on.
options.cost_shape: Flat and predictable: a small fixed monthly amount that grows with allocated resources, not with requests.
options.becomes_the_answer_if: the app needs websockets/realtime, background workers or cron (rule 3), or the budget needs a flat predictable bill.

options.what: ECS Fargate service behind a load balancer with RDS Postgres in a private subnet, everything defined in CDK (Lambda only for an API-only Python service).
options.why: No existing-cloud, compliance, residency, private-networking or 100x signal is recorded, and it costs a human sooner with low ops capacity — so not proposed on what is known.
options.tradeoffs: Costs a human sooner: someone owns IAM, networking and the CDK stack. First deploy is days, not minutes. Cost depends on the architecture you build, so it needs watching.
options.cost_shape: Architecture-dependent: a baseline for the load balancer, NAT and RDS even at zero traffic, then scales with what you provision.
options.becomes_the_answer_if: the client already runs AWS (rule 1), or a compliance regime, data residency, private networking or a 100x horizon applies (rule 2). Always with CDK.

options.what: Cloud Run service with Cloud SQL Postgres over private IP, defined in Terraform.
options.why: Same ops weight as AWS with less house depth; nothing recorded pulls toward GCP.
options.tradeoffs: Same ops weight as AWS, and the house has less depth here — AWS is the default hyperscaler, so GCP is a client-pulled choice. Worth it when the workload is GCP-native (BigQuery, Vertex, Document AI).
options.cost_shape: Architecture-dependent; Cloud Run scales to zero, Cloud SQL does not.
options.becomes_the_answer_if: the client already runs GCP (rule 1) or the workload is GCP-native — BigQuery, Vertex, Document AI (rule 2).

options.what: Docker Compose on a VM the client runs (Kubernetes only if the client already operates it); Postgres on the host with its own volume.
options.why: Ops capacity is low; self-hosting needs high — someone must own patching, backups and uptime.
options.tradeoffs: You are the platform: patching, uptime, backups, restore drills and on-call are yours. No managed previews or staging unless funded. Only ever a requirement, never a cost play.
options.cost_shape: Hardware or VM rental plus the human time to run it — the second term dominates.
options.becomes_the_answer_if: data may not leave client premises (rule 5) AND the client funds the ops capacity to run it.
